site.title: Devanshi Shah | Product Manager Portfolio
site.description: Portfolio of Devanshi Shah — product-minded engineer turning messy problems into products people actually use.
site.line: I like turning messy problems into products people actually want to use.
site.about: I'm a product-minded engineer moving into product management. I specialize in turning messy problems into products people actually want to use — from discovery and scope through the interface that has to survive the decision. I stay close to the frontend so the product doesn't die in implementation.
site.philosophyTitle: Clear problems, sharp scope, measurable outcomes
site.philosophy: I start messy, name the user and the moment, and ship the smallest version that still tells the truth. Copy and empty states are strategy. Shipping is a beginning.
site.experienceIntro: A path from shipping interfaces to owning the question of whether they should exist — and for whom.
site.contactLine: Open to product roles and conversations about messy problems

experience.summary: Turned ambiguous founder briefs into shippable scope. Moved the room from “can we build it” to “should this exist, and for whom.”
bullets: Ran discovery with users of half-built tools and wrote specs that include empty states and who a feature is not for.
Stayed close to the frontend so product decisions survived implementation instead of dying in a ticket.
Protected the smallest version that still tells the truth — and named the nice-to-haves as someone else’s roadmap.

experience.summary: Raised the quality floor without turning review into theatre. Design and engineering started shaping work in the same conversation.
bullets: Mentored through review, not rewrite — and asked “why are we building this” as a kindness, not a blocker.
Protected focus: fewer fires, clearer sequencing, and a quality bar that held under deadline.
Brought design and engineering into the same conversation before the interface was already decided.

experience.summary: People started asking about the decision, not just the component. Craft became a default.
bullets: Left code better than I found it, and spotted product questions hiding in “small UI changes.”
Treated empty states, copy, and the last 10% as part of the product — not polish after the fact.

experience.summary: Learned that users do not care about folder structure if the next click is confusing. Shipped real interfaces under real constraints.
bullets: Shipped production UIs and learned that the last 10% is the product.
Finished things. Then watched people actually use them.

projects.name: WordDeck
projects.blurb: A vocabulary studio with quizzes, matching, and a relation graph — because new words lived in scattered notes and nothing remembered how they related.

projects.name: TrackTransactions
projects.blurb: A quiet ledger where rows come first and charts only exist if the rows are honest. Months ended with a feeling; now they end with a picture.

projects.name: PlanMyMeal
projects.blurb: A week of dinners you actually own. AI drafts the plan, you edit it — because dinner is a daily product with terrible discovery.

projects.name: Event desk
projects.blurb: Guests find and book. Organizers create and watch status. Availability is not a later feature — booking is trust.

memories.title: Late Night Piano Chords

memories.title: The Sketchbook on the Train
memories.note: Filling 14 pages of rough wireframes and margin doodles on the morning commute. The most elegant product architecture often starts on wrinkled paper with a ballpoint pen.

memories.title: Warm Chai & Bookmarks

craft.title: Notes on craft
craft.intro: This site is a product as much as a portfolio. The list below is what I treat as non‑negotiable when shipping — security, honesty of data, accessibility, performance, and a codebase that stays changeable.
craft.footnote: Collaborators get the same checklist in the project README. This page is for anyone who wants to see how I think about shipping.

groups.title: Security & trust
groups.intro: Assume the network and the browser are hostile. Protect sessions, uploads, and secrets by default.

items.title: HttpOnly CMS sessions with revocation
items.why: Cookies are signed and bound to a session version that bumps on password change — stolen cookies stop working when credentials rotate.

items.title: Same-origin checks on mutating CMS APIs
items.why: Authenticated POSTs verify origin in addition to the session cookie, so cross-site callers can’t casually drive the CMS.

items.title: Path confinement & SSRF guards
items.why: Resume paths stay under uploads; remote fetches only hit public HTTPS hosts (LinkedIn allowlisted). No reading env files via ../ tricks.

items.title: Secrets encrypted at rest, never in the client
items.why: Piano media URLs are encrypted in the database and only played through a same-origin proxy. Encrypt fails closed if the key is missing.

items.title: Upload content sniffing (not MIME trust)
items.why: Images, video, and PDFs are validated by magic bytes. Renamed executables don’t get stored as “photos.”

items.title: Durable rate limits
items.why: Login, password reset, contact, AI generate, and uploads share Upstash Redis limits across serverless instances.

groups.title: Honest data — no fake portfolio content
groups.intro: Empty means empty. Visitors and operators should never confuse placeholders with live CMS data.

items.title: No hardcoded memory fallbacks
items.why: The Memory Jar shows an empty state when the database has no memories — it does not invent sample stories.

items.title: Strict CMS save validation
items.why: Zod rejects incomplete saves instead of quietly inventing names, roles, or untitled projects.

items.title: Destructive seed is gated
items.why: Seeding refuses production unless explicitly allowed, and refuses to overwrite an existing site without FORCE_SEED.

groups.title: Architecture that stays changeable
groups.intro: Clear boundaries keep security-sensitive code out of the browser and keep features easy to extend.

items.title: server / hooks / lib split
items.why: Prisma, auth, crypto, and AI live in server/; client hooks are isolated; lib stays shared utilities and thin API clients.

items.title: Thin AI routes, fat services
items.why: Generate endpoints only gate and respond; Gemini calls and prompts live in server/ai so routes don’t copy-paste.

items.title: Normalized content model
items.why: Site, hero, and theme are separate tables — not one mega-row of unrelated columns.

items.title: CMS admin composed from hooks
items.why: Document state, navigation, and uploads are hooks — AdminApp orchestrates screens instead of owning every concern.

items.title: Homepage as section islands
items.why: About, experience, projects, skills, and contact are separate components so the home shell stays small.

groups.title: Performance, SEO & accessibility
groups.intro: Craft includes what people feel: speed, discoverability, and whether the UI works with a keyboard and a screen reader.

items.title: Tagged content cache + revalidation
items.why: Public pages aren’t force-dynamic forever; CMS saves invalidate a cache tag so readers get fresh copy without a DB hit every time.

items.title: next/image with a safe fallback
items.why: Local and allowlisted remotes are optimized; arbitrary CMS URLs fall back to instead of crashing the page.

items.title: SSR for interactive heroes
items.why: World / Nook / Studio art can render on the server for LCP; shared hooks own piano playback and tilt.

items.title: SEO basics done properly
items.why: metadataBase, Open Graph, Twitter cards, robots.txt, and sitemap.xml — including this page.

items.title: Dialog focus management
items.why: The Memory Jar reveal traps focus, restores it on close, and locks body scroll — Escape still works.

items.title: CMS fields have real labels
items.why: Admin form rows wire htmlFor / id / aria-describedby so assistive tech can name every control.

groups.title: Production hygiene
groups.intro: Small ops details that keep deploys boring — in a good way.

items.title: Blob storage for CMS media
items.why: Production uploads go to Vercel Blob; local disk is a dev fallback and is gitignored.

items.title: Tracked .env.example, ignored secrets
items.why: Clones get a complete template; real .env files never ship in git.

items.title: No SVG uploads in the CMS
items.why: Icons are PNG/WebP/JPEG — SVG as a public document is an XSS footgun we chose not to leave open.
